content.title: About
content.content: Cacti are succulent plants adapted to arid environments. Cooked cactus without added fat is a tender, slightly crunchy stem portion commonly used in Mexican and Mediterranean dishes. It has a mild, faintly sweet flavor and low calorie density.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The edible parts of most cacti are found in the stem, not the spines.
Cooked cactus (nopales) is a traditional ingredient in Mexican dishes such as “nopalitos”.
Cacti can store water, so their nutritional profile varies with growing conditions.
In some cultures cactus symbolizes resilience and strength.
Spiny parts are often used decoratively but are not edible.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Cooked cactus provides very few calories, making it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber in cactus supports digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Cactus contains vitamin C, which aids immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phytochemicals in cactus help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports electrolyte balance
items.content: Potassium and magnesium in cactus contribute to proper fluid balance.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cactus.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Cactus can contain oxalates, which in excess may promote kidney stone formation.

items.title: Toxicity of certain species
items.content: Not all cactus species are edible; some contain toxic compounds and require proper preparation.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Improper cooking can allow bacterial growth, so ensure the cactus is fully cooked.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked cactus can be served as a side dish, added to salads, soups, omelets, or used as a filling for tacos. It is often sliced into rings and lightly sautéed without oil to enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked cactus in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags to preserve texture and taste.

content.title: About
content.content: Oat squares are crunchy cereal pieces made from whole oat groats, typically shaped as squares. They are produced from whole oats, sugar, salt, and sometimes added ingredients such as dried fruit or nuts. The product is often enjoyed as a quick breakfast or snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oat squares are commonly called “oat squares” in Russia and other CIS countries.
Oats, the base ingredient, are one of the oldest cultivated grains.
Unlike many breakfast cereals, oat squares usually contain no artificial flavors.
Oats are rich in beta‑glucan, a soluble fiber that supports heart health.
Some versions are fortified with B‑vitamins and iron.

items.title: Rich in beta‑glucan
items.content: Beta‑glucan helps lower cholesterol levels and supports the immune system.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs provide sustained energy and a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and helps regulate blood sugar.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2 and B6 are involved in carbohydrate metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many other dry cereals, oat squares have a modest fat content.

items.title: Oat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to oats or to added ingredients such as nuts.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Certain varieties contain added sugar, which should be considered by people with diabetes or low‑sugar diets.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Oats are often processed on equipment that also handles gluten; those with celiac disease should choose certified gluten‑free oat squares.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Oat squares can be eaten dry, added to milk, yogurt, or kefir. They are also used in granola mixes, desserts, and energy bars. For a softer texture, pour hot milk over them and let them sit for a few minutes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a sealed package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For longer shelf life, keep in the refrigerator to prevent moisture and spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: A chicken drumstick is the lower part of the thigh, containing meat, skin, and a small bone. When sauteed, the skin becomes crisp while the meat stays juicy. The product is rich in protein, B‑vitamins, and minerals such as iron and zinc.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken drumsticks are a staple in many cuisines, from American BBQ to Asian stir‑fries.
Leaving the skin on during cooking adds flavor, texture, and beneficial fatty acids.
The "saute" method first sears the drumstick on high heat, then finishes it at a lower temperature for even cooking.
Drumsticks are easier to cook to a safe internal temperature than breast meat because of their higher fat content.
In some cultures, chicken drumsticks are considered a celebratory dish served at special occasions.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 20 g of complete protein, essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains niacin (B3), vitamin B6, and riboflavin (B2), which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals: iron and zinc
items.content: Iron aids oxygen transport, while zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Beneficial fats in the skin
items.content: The skin supplies monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that can be heart‑healthy when eaten in moderation.

items.title: Collagen content
items.content: Chicken skin is a source of collagen, which may benefit skin, joint, and connective‑tissue health.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked drumsticks may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter. Cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C (165 °F).

items.title: High sodium if salted
items.content: Added salt during cooking increases sodium intake, which can be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Although uncommon, some individuals may be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: The skin contains saturated fat; frequent consumption should be balanced with overall dietary fat intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drumsticks can be sauteed in a little oil, baked, or braised in sauces. The skin is usually left on for flavor and crunch. Serve with vegetables, rice, potatoes, or salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Raw drumsticks keep in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Cooked pieces can be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days or frozen for up to 3 months.

infant-formula-store-brand-added-rice.title: Infant formula, store brand, added rice

content.title: About
content.content: Infant formula with added rice is a ready‑to‑use powdered milk for babies from 6 months onward, enriched with essential vitamins, minerals and easily digestible rice carbohydrates. Produced under a store brand, it meets national and international safety standards for infant nutrition.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rice in the formula helps smooth digestion and reduces the risk of constipation in infants.
The blend contains DHA and ARA – important fatty acids for brain and eye development.
The product has undergone clinical testing confirming its safety and nutritional adequacy.
Packaging usually includes preparation instructions and age recommendations.
Store brands often provide a more affordable price while maintaining quality.

items.title: Supports growth and development
items.content: Provides the baby with the necessary proteins, fats and carbs to promote normal growth and organ development.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These trace minerals are vital for immune function and cognitive performance.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Helps with energy production and supports the nervous system.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Aid in building strong bone tissue.

items.title: Easily digestible carbohydrate source
items.content: Rice starch provides a steady glucose supply for the infant.

items.title: Cow‑milk protein allergy
items.content: Some infants may react to the bovine milk proteins present in the formula.

items.title: Improper reconstitution
items.content: A solution that is too concentrated can strain the baby’s kidneys.

items.title: Shelf life after opening
items.content: Prepared formula should be used within 24 hours; otherwise bacterial growth risk increases.

items.title: Storage in hot climates
items.content: High temperatures may degrade nutrient quality.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Mix the powder with warm (not hot) water according to the label instructions, typically 1 tsp per 30 ml of water. Stir until smooth, let it cool to body temperature, and feed the baby immediately.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened containers in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the bag tightly sealed and use within 24 hours. Discard if you notice off‑odors, discoloration or clumping.

content.title: About
content.content: Stuffed pepper with rice is a vegetable dish where a sweet bell pepper is filled with a mixture of cooked rice, vegetables, spices, and sometimes cheese. The dish is completely meat‑free, making it suitable for vegetarians and anyone looking for a light yet satisfying dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stuffed peppers are popular in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and Latin American cuisines.
Traditional recipes often include tomato paste, giving the filling a rich color and flavor.
Peppers are high in vitamin C – one medium pepper provides more than 100 % of the daily requirement.
The recipe can be easily adapted with beans, nuts, or meat substitutes for extra protein.
In Russia, stuffed peppers are frequently served as a baked casserole topped with a cheese crust.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity, supports collagen synthesis, and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Rice supplies slow‑releasing energy, helping to maintain satiety.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Prepared without meat and with minimal oil, the dish fits low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Both pepper and rice provide fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Carotenoids in red and yellow peppers have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Pepper allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to capsaicin found in peppers.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If ready‑made sauces are used, the dish can become high in salt; monitor added sodium.

items.title: Dietary restrictions
items.content: People avoiding gluten should check that spices and sauces are gluten‑free.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Halve the peppers, remove seeds, stuff with the rice mixture, optionally sprinkle grated cheese, and bake for 20‑25 minutes at 180 °C until the top is golden. Serve hot, often with tomato sauce or fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked stuffed peppers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly before serving.
